sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Medicine Ball Push Up is an advanced bodyweight pushing exercise that increases instability by placing both hands on a medicine ball.

Balancing on the ball forces the stabiliser muscles of the shoulders, chest, and core to work harder than a standard push up.

This variation is excellent for developing chest strength, improving balance, and building functional upper body stability.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Increased chest activation due to the narrow hand position on the ball
- Greater core engagement from the unstable surface
- Improved shoulder stabilisation and joint integrity
- Enhanced proprioception and balance
- Builds grip and wrist strength
- Develops functional pushing power
- Requires no gym — only a medicine ball and floor space

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Chest (Pectoralis Major)

Secondary: Triceps, Anterior Deltoids, Core (Rectus Abdominis, Obliques), Serratus Anterior, Forearms

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Place a medicine ball on the floor in front of you.
2. Kneel down and place both hands on top of the medicine ball directly under your chest.
3. Extend your legs behind you into a plank position.
4. Your body should form a straight line from head to heels.
5. Engage your core and squeeze your glutes to maintain a rigid torso.
6. Grip the sides of the ball firmly with your fingers for stability.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Place both hands on the medicine ball directly under your chest.
2. Press yourself up until your arms are fully extended while maintaining a neutral spine, straight back position.
3. Lower yourself back down until your chest touches the back of your hands on the medicine ball.
4. Repeat for reps.
5. Keep your elbows close to your body throughout the movement.
6. Move slowly and with control — the instability of the ball requires focus.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Placing hands too far forward on the ball instead of directly under the chest
- Letting the hips sag or pike upward, breaking the plank position
- Rushing through reps without controlling the balance
- Not lowering fully until the chest touches the hands
- Flaring the elbows wide instead of keeping them tucked
- Using a ball that is too large or too small for comfortable hand placement
- Not engaging the core, causing the lower back to arch

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Medicine Ball (6-14 lbs recommended)
- A flat, stable floor surface
- Optional: Exercise mat for comfort
- Optional: Non-slip mat under the ball for extra stability
- Ensure the medicine ball has a textured or grippy surface

sections.heading: Choosing Your Medicine Ball
sections.content:
1. Select a ball that is firm enough to support your weight without excessive compression.
2. A slightly larger ball (10-12 inch diameter) is easier to balance on.
3. Rubber or textured surfaces provide better grip than smooth leather.
4. Start with a lighter ball to learn the balance before progressing.
5. Avoid slam balls that are too soft — they compress and make balancing difficult.
6. The ball should sit flat on the floor without rolling.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Hands: Both placed firmly on top of the medicine ball, gripping the sides.
2. Arms: Directly under the chest, elbows close to the body.
3. Core: Braced tight to maintain a flat back throughout.
4. Glutes: Squeezed to keep hips level.
5. Feet: Together or slightly apart for additional balance.
6. Head: Neutral position, looking slightly ahead.
7. Shoulders: Depressed and away from the ears.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Standard Push Up: Stable surface, same pushing pattern
- Close Grip Push Up: Narrow hand placement on the floor for triceps emphasis
- Bosu Ball Push Up: Similar instability challenge with a larger surface
- Dumbbell Push Up: Hands on dumbbells for neutral wrist position
- Decline Push Up: Feet elevated to increase difficulty
- Incline Push Up: Hands elevated for an easier variation

sections.heading: Medicine Ball Push Up Variations
sections.content:
Medicine Ball Push Up: Both hands on one ball, standard variation
Alternating Medicine Ball Push Up: One hand on ball, alternate each rep
Staggered Medicine Ball Push Up: One hand on ball, one on floor
Medicine Ball Diamond Push Up: Hands in diamond shape on ball
Elevated Feet Medicine Ball Push Up: Feet on bench for added difficulty
Slow Tempo Medicine Ball Push Up: 3-4 second eccentric for time under tension

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Wrist Pain: Ensure proper grip on ball sides, try push up handles on floor instead
Shoulder Discomfort: Reduce range of motion or switch to incline push ups
Balance Difficulty: Start with wider foot placement for more stability
Lack of Strength: Begin with incline medicine ball push ups using a bench
Core Weakness: Practice plank holds on the medicine ball before adding push ups
Learning Stage: Master standard push ups first, then progress to the medicine ball
